entries.title: Pakistan-Taliban conflict: How India could benefit from shifting regional dynamics
entries.summary: As Pakistan's influence in Afghanistan comes under strain, India is rebuilding ties with the Taliban in Kabul. Can New Delhi turn this diplomatic opening into lasting strategic gains?
entries.content:
India

Does Pakistan-Taliban conflict create a strategic opening for India?

October 21, 2026

As Pakistan's influence in Afghanistan comes under strain, India is rebuilding ties with the Taliban in Kabul. Can New Delhi turn this diplomatic opening into lasting strategic gains?

Pakistan and Afghanistan right now are locked in a cycle of escalating tension. Repeated border clashes have strained ties between the two nations. 

The current round of tensions began in February 2026, when Pakistan launched strikes into Afghanistan targeting Taliban militants. At one point in March, Pakistan's defense minister said the country was at "open war" with Afghanistan. Periodic bouts of violence have continued since then, with the latest Pakistani strikes targeting the Afghan Taliban's "terrorist hubs" reported earlier in October.

At the heart of the dispute is Pakistan's accusation that the Taliban authorities in Kabul allow the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group, to target Pakistan from Afghan territory. Kabul denies providing the group with sanctuary.

Where does India come into play?

As the two neighbors trade strikes, the escalating conflict "presents a significant diplomatic and strategic opportunity for India," Shanthie Mariet D'Souza, an Afghanistan expert and founder of the India-based Mantraya Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.

D'Souza argues the confrontation has weakened Pakistan's traditional influence in Afghanistan and encouraged the Taliban to broaden its external relations.

"India can respond by expanding diplomatic engagement, humanitarian assistance, development projects and trade, while seeking assurances that Afghan territory will not be used by anti-India militant groups," she said.

However, D'Souza cautioned against interpreting the opening as a fundamental realignment.

"There is no ideological alignment between India and the Taliban," she said. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is likely to pursue a diversified foreign policy rather than align exclusively with New Delhi.

India also lacks the geographical advantages, economic leverage and security presence needed to replace Pakistan's influence, she notes. "The scenario of the Taliban becoming a strategic ally remains far-fetched."

Former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan Amar Sinha warned against viewing the conflict simply as an opportunity for New Delhi to gain at Pakistan's expense.

"The issues have very little to do with India," Sinha told DW, arguing that India was not seeking strategic advantage from the fighting. He also pointed to the consequences of Pakistan's military actions for Afghan civilians.

"Yet the rupture has made Kabul's search for alternative partners more pressing," he added.

For India, that creates an opening, but not necessarily a strategic alignment, Sinha notes. The Taliban can seek Indian assistance while maintaining relations with China, Russia, Iran and Gulf states, preserving its autonomy rather than exchanging dependence on Pakistan for dependence on India.

The cost of closer ties

Gautam Mukhopadhyaya, another former Indian ambassador to Afghanistan, sees the deterioration in relations between Pakistan and the Taliban as an opportunity for India to recover some of the strategic ground it lost when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

"The crisis has allowed strategic openings for India," Mukhopadhyaya told DW. He warned, however, that New Delhi's own treatment of Afghans could undermine its efforts to build a durable relationship.

He pointed to restrictions affecting Afghans seeking Indian visas for education, scholarships, work and medical treatment.

"For all practical purposes, India's security establishment treats Afghans as proxy Pakistanis and 'terrorists' by default," he said.

Former Afghan partners had been left "disappointed, even bitter," Mukhopadhyaya added. "A strategic relationship built on the sands of oppression is not a sound foundation."

Trade cannot overcome geography

India has restored air freight links between Kabul and Delhi and between Kabul and Amritsar in northwestern India in December 2025.

Bilateral trade between India and Afghanistan stood at about $908 million (€807 million) in the 2025-26 fiscal year, while trade between Pakistan and Afghanistan fell sharply amid repeated border closures.

On October 14, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi stressed the importance of relations with India during talks with Indian charge d'affaires Yatin Patel, signaling Kabul's interest in expanding economic cooperation.

But air freight is expensive, and India cannot easily replace Pakistan as a transit route.

New Delhi has sought to use Iran's Chabahar port to improve access to Afghanistan and Central Asia, but regional instability and complications surrounding Iran have constrained those ambitions.

D'Souza cautioned that "the ongoing conflict in Iran" limits India's ability to use Chabahar as a crucial trade and connectivity hub.

Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University specializing in Afghanistan and Eurasian connectivity, highlighted similar obstacles.

"In the last few decades, Islamabad has obstructed Kabul's efforts to gain access to the vast Indian market. However, political instability in Afghanistan and sanctions on Iran have undermined these efforts," Sachdeva told DW.

"Afghanistan's potential as a connector between regional markets remains considerable, but the infrastructure and political conditions needed to realize it are far from assured," he added.

Sachdeva also sees Russia and China as better positioned to shape Afghanistan's wider economic integration. Alternative routes may become more attractive to India, but they are not commercially viable overnight.

Islamabad's security fears

Pakistan has portrayed arch-rival India's growing engagement with the Taliban as a security threat. On October 7, Pakistani diplomat Muhammad Jawad Ajmal accused India at the United Nations of providing the Taliban with material and logistical support.

"Under the guise of humanitarian aid, they have been actively supporting the Taliban regime with material and logistical support for carrying out terrorist attacks against Pakistan," Ajmal said.

The allegation reflects Islamabad's position and has not been established as fact.

Pakistan has accused India of supporting the TTP and the Balochistan Liberation Army, a militant organization.

India rejects accusations of backing militant activity, while the Taliban denies allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.

Ayesha Siddiqa, a Pakistani expert on military and security affairs at King's College London, offered a more nuanced assessment of Pakistan's position.

"India has stepped into a space and is trying to exert its influence and feed anti-Pakistan groups intelligence," she told DW.

Siddiqa added that Pakistan's establishment continues to view the crisis through "a singular security lens."

"Islamabad feels physically squeezed from both sides," she said, adding that closer Kabul-New Delhi ties could create "a dangerous two-front security trap" for Pakistan.

India may gain more room to operate in Afghanistan as ties between Kabul and Islamabad deteriorate. But the Taliban is unlikely to put all its eggs in New Delhi's basket.

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard during Witkoff talks
entries.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces years ago in Ukraine.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russia frees jailed American Stephen Hubbard

Published October 21, 2026last updated October 21, 2026

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces years ago in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday.

Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024.

Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family."

US President Donald Trump later said that he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week.

"The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release."

However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions, which he said was a necessary concession.

"If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said.

Putin, Witkoff to discuss Ukraine peace deal

The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administreation as the two sides discuss a peace deal in Ukraine.

"We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin.

Putin proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow, and the possibility of trilateral talks with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin —comes a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway, which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as "positive."

"He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to ‌go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and ‌let's ​see if we can make some progress," he said ahead of the talks.

Witkoff to return to Oslo

Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy and other European leaders in Oslo has brought fresh momentum to peace efforts, more than 4 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg.

"I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning.

Nevertheless, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow was willing to listen but that he didn't expect any "miracle." Trump on Tuesday reiterated that he wants Zelenskyy "to make a deal."

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: UK approves Jackdaw gas field after years in limbo
entries.summary: Drilling is set to begin in the controversial North Sea plot as the government seeks to tackle high energy costs. Environmental groups have criticized the move and called for more clean energy.
entries.content:
October 21, 2026

Drilling is set to begin in the controversial North Sea plot as the government seeks to tackle high energy costs. Environmental groups have criticized the move and called for more clean energy.

The UK government gave its approval for drilling to begin in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on Wednesday following years of legal and political problems that had blocked the controversial fossil fuel venture.

The Labour government justified the move saying it would strengthen the UK's energy security amid rising energy costs due to the US-Israeli war against Iran.

The gas field had previously been approved by the previous Conservative government, but wes held up by a Scottish court that said the approval had failed to consider carbon emissions.

The field lies about 150 miles (240 kilometres) east of Aberdeen in Scotland.

What did the UK government say about the Jackdaw approval?

Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to increase drilling in the North Sea, said the new gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm this winter."

"At a time when people are really struggling, it's right that we look in a responsible way at maximising the existing energy reserves we have in Britain that could help," he said.

"We're committed to moving towards renewable energy and reaching net zero by 2050. But even on our ambitious climate path, we'll still require oil and gas as part of our energy needs for decades to come. That's why we're taking a pragmatic approach to the North Sea," Burnham added.

Energy Minister Miatta Fahnbulleh said gas could start flowing to British houses and businesses by the end of the month. It is expected that Jackdaw will increase domestic gas production by 6% and run for 11 years.

What has been the reaction to the UK's new gas project?

Shell, which is part of the Adura joint venture along with Norway's Equinor, welcomed the decision.

"Long-term energy projects depend on a competitive and stable investment environment, alongside timely and predictable regulatory decisions," Shell said.

However, the move has also been met with strong criticism. The Green Party called it "climate vandalism," while Greenpeace said the approval showed "the toxic grip fossil fuel lobbyists still hold over our energy policy."

"True pragmatism means severing our reliance on expensive oil and gas that leaves British households broke, supercharges extreme weather, and leaves our energy security at the mercy of petrostates," said the environmental group's Ami McCarthy.

Critics have also questioned whether the new project would indeed have an impact on British gas bills since prices are determined by global energy markets.

In an attempt to show the government's commitment to its climate targets, alongside the Jackdaw approval, it announced the set up of a new Energy Wealth Fund, with an initial £2 billion ($2.7 billion), aimed at channeling oil and gas revenues into funding the transition to cleaner energy.

The UK is targeting net zero emissions by 2050, although this target must be examined under the realities already facing the planet, with a new UN report saying the world is heading for 2.8 degrees of warming, way beyond the 1.5 degrees target set in the Paris Climate Agreement.

It also comes after the UK experienced its hottest ever summer on record, with temperatures hitting previously unheard of 38 degrees in some areas in June, according to the Met Office.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: US sanctions target Iran's rail sector as Tehran shifts cargo from sea routes to overland corridors
entries.summary: As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.
entries.content:
October 21, 2026

As US sanctions expand to Iran's rail sector, Tehran is relying more heavily on overland links with China and Central Asia. But capacity constraints, delays and costs limit rail's ability to replace maritime trade.

The United States has opened another front in its economic pressure campaign against Iran, this time targeting the railways Tehran increasingly relies on as maritime trade becomes more difficult.

On October 1, the US Treasury sanctioned three Iranian railway companies alongside seven automakers and five foreign suppliers of automotive parts as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.

Washington says Iran's rail and automotive industries provide revenue and logistical capacity to the state and are connected to networks involving the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The timing of the move is significant. Since the US maritime blockade sharply restricted Iran's southern trade routes, Tehran has tried to move more goods through its land borders and railway connections with China, Central Asia, Russia and Turkey.

Rail transport has become more important just as Washington decided to target it.

Iran expands regional rail links

Shahriar Naghizadeh, director general for foreign trade at Iran's railway authority, was quoted by the semi-official Mehr news agency as saying that the country has around 15,000 kilometers (9,300 miles) of main and secondary railway lines, more than 35,000 wagons and nearly 500 diesel locomotives.

The network carried around 44 million tons of freight in the Iranian year ending in March 2026, up from about 40 million tons the previous year, according to Naghizadeh. And authorities are targeting 54 million tons this year.

Iran is linked to neighboring markets through 13 rail crossings, providing overland access to Turkey, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and onward routes to Central Asia and China via Turkmenistan.

The new US sanctions raise questions about how foreign railway operators, freight forwarders, banks and insurers will continue dealing with Iranian rail companies.

China-Iran rail traffic expands

Bloomberg reported in May that freight trains traveling from the Chinese city of Xi'an to Tehran had increased from around one per week before the US blockade to roughly one every three or four days.

In September, a train left China carrying automotive parts, consumer goods and other cargo. It ran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan before entering Iran at Sarakhs with an expected transit time of 14 to 16 days.

For Iran, such services offer a route to Chinese suppliers that avoids the area around the Strait of Hormuz. But advertised transit times do not necessarily reflect what an importer experiences.

Delivery date cannot be guaranteed

A Chinese freight company told DW that actual delivery times can stretch far beyond advertised schedules because of border inspections, customs procedures and train availability.

It estimated that rail transit along the main route from western China to Tehran would take 50-60 days under current conditions. Road transport along a similar route is around 22 to 25 days.

The gap between a scheduled 14-day transit time and commercial estimates of up to 60 days highlights one of the central challenges facing Iran.

Customs inspections, gauge changes, payment problems and sanctions can all be another potential point of delay.

Increasing the number of trains also requires more locomotives, wagons and cooperation from several transit countries.

Rail works best for critical inputs

Alireza Salavati, managing director of London-based Middle East Analytica, said rail is increasingly useful for Iran but should not be mistaken as a replacement for maritime trade.

"A workable overland route now links China and Iran, but I would not call it a replacement for sea freight," he told DW.

Under normal conditions, ships can move far larger quantities at lower unit costs. Rail becomes more attractive for goods where speed and continuity matter more than the cheapest transport.

That includes automotive components, machinery, electronics and industrial inputs, whose absence can stop an entire production line.

When delays become a cash problem

Salavati argues that the effect on companies cannot be measured only in freight charges.

For a manufacturer importing $1 million (€890,000) worth of inputs every 30 days, a 30-day journey means roughly a million dollars of inventory may be tied up in transit.

Cutting the journey to 15 days could reduce that amount significantly, depending on payment arrangements. The reverse can be much more damaging.

If input costs rise while delivery times stretch from 30 to 45 days, companies need more working capital simply to maintain the same production flow, the expert explained, pointing out that a factory can have customers and orders but still have to reduce production because too much cash is trapped in goods that have not arrived.

"Reliability matters as much as speed," Salavati said. "A 15-day train is little use if the container waits a week to depart, or if the bank or insurer will not touch it."

The new US sanctions add another source of uncertainty to that calculation.

Sanctions push trade toward other corridors

Optimizing its railway use would give Iran more options than having to rely on southern ports alone, but the overall scale remains limited.

Washington's sanction strategy is designed to isolate Iran by closing maritime, financial, aviation and now railway channels.

Still, Salavati argues that the same pressure may accelerate Iran's integration with alternative networks.

"Washington's efforts to isolate Iran may also be pushing it deeper than at any point in recent years into China's economic orbit and closer to Russia's wartime strategic system," he said.

That does not mean China or Russia can make up for the economic cost of US pressure, since Iranian importers still need insurers, banks and customers able to absorb higher prices.

Container trains can only carry a fraction of what a large cargo vessel can transport, so for now, rail provides Iran with a limited alternative trade channel.

Its wider success depends on better financing and becoming more reliable — but even then it is not a wholesale substitute for sea freight.

Edited by: Tim Rooks

entries.title: Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack as suspect appears in court
entries.summary: Doctors have amputated both of Helen Haines legs after the Australian lawmaker was hit in an apparent deliberate attack. The suspected driver involved in the attack has appeared in court.
entries.content:
Australia

Australian MP Helen Haines loses both legs after car attack

Published October 19, 2026last updated October 21, 2026

Doctors have amputated both of Helen Haines legs after the Australian lawmaker was hit in an apparent deliberate attack. The suspected driver involved in the attack has appeared in court.

Helen Haines, an Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday, has lost both of her legs, her husband said on Wednesday.

Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

A 43-year-old suspect, Brendan N. from nearby Tarrawingee, appeared in Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged with intentionally causing serious injury, dangerous driving causing serious injury and causing harm to a federal official.

Haines loses both legs after apparent attack

The independent MP underwent surgery on Monday night after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that her left leg had been amputated.

Doctors then proceeded to amputate her right leg on Wednesday after having tried to save it.

"The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family," Phil Haines told reporters in Melbourne.

"We are grateful and thankful that at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape," he said.

What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?

Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. Later reports from witnesses said that after first pinning Haines against her own car, the driver reversed and rammed into her a second time.

The driver was arrested shortly after, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.

The suspect's lawyer, Chirag Patel, told Magistrate Allison Vaughan on Wednesday that his client suffers from a rare neurological condition, as well as an undiagnosed mental health condition. He also said the defendant was suffering from a concussion.

Local barber ran to assist

Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.

Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.

"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't ​pull it ‌out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.

Jefferies said he then held the man down until ‌police arrived.

"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and ‌he was ​no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.

Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."

"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.

Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese

Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.

"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."

At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.

Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.

Edited by: Karl Sexton and Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Germany news: 'Tech error' brings early cigarette tax hike
entries.summary: Germany's Finance Ministry has said the tax hike went into effect months early due to a "technical error." AfD co-Chair Alice Weidel will present "A New Deal for Europe" in Strasbourg. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: 'Tech error' brings early cigarette tax hike

Published October 21, 2026last updated October 21, 2026

Germany's Finance Ministry has said the tax hike went into effect months early due to a "technical error." AfD co-Chair Alice Weidel will present "A New Deal for Europe" in Strasbourg. Follow DW for the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's Finance Ministry has erroneously introduced an approved tax hike on tobacco products months before it was scheduled to come into effect

  • A 'technical error' with incorrect dates is said to have caused the flub

  • The issue is further complicated by the fact that tax stamps for the new rate are not yet ready, meaning tobacco companies cannot pay the new, significantly higher rate

  • Alice Weidel of the AfD will pitch what she is calling "A New Deal for Europe" in Strasbourg this afternoon

  • NVIDIA's Jensen Huang will deliver the keynote address at a Berlin AI conference on AI chips, infrastructure, software and robotics

Here is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, October 21, 2026:

Skip next section IDF says it killed Hamas member involved in abduction of German dual national

IDF says it killed Hamas member involved in abduction of German dual national

The Israel Defense Forces (IFD) said in a post on X that they have killed Tamer Mohammad Ibrahim Al-Zabaq, a member of the Hamas terror group who was involved in the October 7 attacks.

The post said that al-Zabaq had been one of the men responsible for the abduction of Shani Louk, a dual German-Israeli national.

Louk was initially thought to have been taken hostage following the Hamas-led attacks but it was later confirmed that she had been killed.

In the immediate aftermath of the terror attacks, pictures and videos shared online showed a young woman, believed to be Shani, lying face down in a pick-up truck driven by militants. It was unclear from the footage whether she was alive.

The IDF also accused Al-Zabaq of operating to "restore Hamas' military capabilities, in systematic violation of the ceasefire."

"The terrorist was eliminated in order to remove the threat he posed," the IDF said.

The claims in the X post could not be independently verified.

Israel has carried out numerous deadly strikes on Gaza since the ceasefire came into effect just over a year ago.

Skip next section Merz calls on Trump to make sure South Africa is at G20

Merz calls on Trump to make sure South Africa is at G20

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, addressing the Business Global Dialogue summit in Berlin on Wednesday, renewed calls for US President Donald Trump to invite South Africa (a G20 member) to the upcoming G20 summit that he will host in Miami this December.

"Whoever talks about the future of the global economy must include all important partners. Of course Africa belongs at the table," he said, adding: "The African Union is a G20 member, as is South Africa. That is why I urgently insist that South Africa be represented at the G20 summit."

Merz made a similar plea last year, when Trump angrily insisted that he would not invite South Africa to the annual summit of the 20 leading industrial and emerging economies.

Trump has accused South Africa of committing genocide on white farmers and dismissed South African pushback against his repeated claim. The anti-immigrant president also took the unusual step of offering South Africans political asylum in the US — as long as they are white.

The US President is apparently less bothered by wars of aggression, extending an invitation to President Vladimir Putin to come to Miami, despite Russia being thrown out of the G8 — now G7 — over its 2014 invasion and annexation of Ukraine's Crimea.

Beyond his plea for South Africa's inclusion, Merz said he would travel to the US with what he called a "Miami Growth Agenda" aimed at slashing bureaucracy, pushing structural reforms and making investment easier.

"Those" he said, "are the prerequisites for new economic growth and prosperity, not only in Germany, but globally."

Skip next section Russia arrests German national, says he's a 'mercenary' — reports

Russia arrests German national, says he's a 'mercenary' — reports

Russian FSB agents have arrested a German national, accusing him of being a mercenary under contract with the Ukrainian army.

"The Federal Security Service of the Russian Federation has detained a German citizen who is a serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine," said a statement cited by Russian news agencies.

The FSB says the man, whom they described as a sniper, previously fought in Afghanistan and Syria as well as in Ukraine between 2016 and 2018.

They say he arrived in Ukraine last November and signed a three-year contract with the Ukrainian army before deserting over unpaid wages.

Last week, the FSB arrested a Swedish national whom Russian authorities also accused of fighting on Kyiv's behalf.

Russia has arrested hundreds of foreign nationals that it accuses of "espionage," "sabotage" or "treason" to long prison sentences since it began its invasion of neighboring Ukraine. 

A number of foreign nationals have also been jailed over supposed "mercenary activity."

Skip next section Feminist Alice Schwarzer announces closure of Emma magazine

Feminist Alice Schwarzer announces closure of Emma magazine

Alice Schwarzer, Germany's most famous feminist, told DPA on Wednesday that the December 8 issue of her magazine Emma would be its last.

Schwarzer said despite dwindling circulation, the magazine is still turning a profit but the 83-year-old said "we are leaving because we think: Enough is enough!" 

She said that Emma had stood up against "quite a bit of nonsense in the name of feminism," adding, "we are exhausted."

The first issue of Emma hit newsstands on January 26, 1977, with Schwarzer saying hostility against women in "men's media" had driven her to found a magazine that was produced by women, for women.

Schwarzer on Wednesday described Emma as the world's last professional, feminist-owned magazine still on newsstands.



Child sexual abuse and Islamism were among the issues that Emma began covering from the beginning. It later expanded to look at German tax law as regards married couples, breast cancer and female genital mutilation, among other topics. 

Among the controversial stances that Schwarzer has taken over the years, two that hurt sales were her seemingly pro-Russian calls for a quick peace deal with Ukraine after the start of Moscow's 2022 invasion — leading 20% of readers to cancel subscriptions — and her perceived hostility on transgender issues.

Schwarzer wholly rejects accusations that she has made transphobic, racist and misogynistic statements.

Emma's extensive archive will now be transferred to the German Literature Archive in Marbach, where it will be publicly accessible.

Asked about what people may not understand looking back, Schwarzer pointed to the hardships that women had to overcome in order to secure the rights enjoyed by women today.

Skip next section Tobacco tax introduced months early

Tobacco tax introduced months early

Germany's Finance Ministry said that a "technical error" had led to the early introduction of a steep tax hike on tobacco products.

The hike received final parliamentary approval on Friday and had been scheduled to go into effect at the turn of the year.

Instead the changes officially gazetted on Tuesday stated that they would come into force on Wednesday.

"A technical error occurred in the documents regarding the effective date," said the Ministry, adding that a correction had been initiated.

The changes are expected to pump some €12 billion ($13.5 billion) in added tax revenue over the next four years.

However, tobacco companies will be unable to pay the higher rate due to the fact that new tax stamps are not yet available.

Currently, a 20-pack of cigarettes costs around €8-€10. The Finance Ministry expects that price to rise to between €12 and €14 per pack.

Roughly 1-in-5 people (19%) smoke in Germany, with around 130,000 dying of tobacco-related illness each year.

Although health experts and politicians hope that higher prices will deter people from smoking, the German Customs Union and the tobacco industry warn that smokers could simply turn to contraband cigarettes instead.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn where we start the day looking at a cigarette tax hike that has gone into effect months before scheduled after "a technical error."

The price hike was supposed to happen at the beginning of 2028 but will now start today.

In Strasbourg, France, Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-Chair Alice Weidel will hold a press conference announcing what she has billed "A New Deal for Europe." AfD EU Parliamentarians Rene Aust and Alexander Sell will accompany her. 

Stay tuned for this and more from DW …

entries.title: Football: German coach Hürzeler flying high in Premier League
entries.summary: Fabian Hürzeler is younger than his star player, a fellow Premier League German. But, contrary to his reputation in his homeland, Hürzeler has become a popular figure both on and off the pitch in England.

entries.title: India news: India-US trade deal 'pretty close,' says Trump
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump hinted that the US-India trade deal could look different from the previous ones. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Asia

India news: India-US trade deal 'pretty close,' says Trump

Published October 21, 2026last updated October 21, 2026

US President Donald Trump hinted that the US-India trade deal could look different from the previous ones. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Donald Trump's assurance on the finalization of the India-US trade deal comes Marco Rubio visits India
  • Rubio said that 99 % of the work on the trade deal is complete
  • UN experts have called for an investigation into the police crackdown on protesters in India

Here's a roundup of our coverage from India from Wednesday, October 21:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Rubio says ties with Pakistan, China will never come at India's expense

Rubio says ties with Pakistan, China will never come at India's expense

In an exclusive interview with Indian daily The Indian Express, Rubio said that "our relationship with any country will never come at the expense of India."

"What everyone should be assured of in India is that our relationship, not just with Pakistan but with any country in the world, will never come at the expense of our relationship. We don't view it that way in our relationship with India," he said.

Rubio is currently on a visit to India — his second official trip to the country this year.

Skip next section Delhi High Court questions CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's plea

Delhi High Court questions CJP leaders Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka's plea

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday questioned the pleas filed by Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka challenging proceedings over alleged breaches of bonds to maintain peace

The court allowed Das and Ranka to withdraw their pleas challenging the custody proceedings after both requested permission to do on Wednesday.

Justice Subramonium Prasad, addressing Das and Ranka's counsel Abhik Chimni, observed that the bond furnished on October 10 was allegedly breached the very next day, October 11, according to a report by Indian newspaper The Indian Express.

Chimni argued that Das and Ranka should not have to spend another two days in custody, questioning the legality of the October 19 order which extended their initial five days of judicial custody. He contended that the magistrate lacked jurisdiction to extend their custody.

The CJP leaders were arrested on October 14 for trespassing into Jantar Mantar and hoisting the national flag as a sign of protest. Their extended judicial custody is supposed to end today.

The CJP leadership had called for protests demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner for his alleged role in mass voter roll revisions that led to the deletion of 130 million names from electoral rolls.

Skip next section After three Meiteis, Kuki man shot dead in Manipur

After three Meiteis, Kuki man shot dead in Manipur

A man from the ethnic Kuki community was shot dead in a forested area in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Tuesday, a day after three Meitei villagers were shot dead allegedly by "militants."

The incident occurred when the man and one other person were heading to gather bamboo shoots, according to a report by Indian newspaper The Indian Express.

The victim sustained fatal gunshot injuries and died on the spot, while the other man managed to escape unhurt.

The attacks between the Hindu Meitei majority and largely Christian Kuki minority are the latest in prolonged ethnic violence in Manipur since 2023  over economic benefits and job quotas.

Skip next section UN experts warn of 'excessive' force against protesters in India

UN experts warn of 'excessive' force against protesters in India

United Nations experts on Tuesday called for an independent investigation into Indian authorities' crackdown on protesters, saying demonstrators sustained injuries and some reported being subjected to ill-treatment.

The experts urged Indian authorities to respect, protect, and fulfill the right to peaceful protest and to ensure justice for alleged human rights violations reported during these and previous demonstrations.

"We have repeatedly alerted the Indian authorities to undue restrictions on peaceful assembly, excessive use of force, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, and the targeting of student activists, amongst others," the experts said.

"Despite the non-violent nature of the assemblies, law enforcement agencies have reportedly deployed force against unarmed students, including lathi charges and have prevented thousands from joining the protests," the experts added.

The statement by the UN experts follows a police crackdown on protesters in Delhi who are demanding the resignation of India's election chief, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged vote theft and mass voter deletions from electoral rolls.

Skip next section India, US "pretty close" to finalising a trade deal: Donald Trump

India, US "pretty close" to finalising a trade deal: Donald Trump

US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said that Washington and New Delhi are pretty close to concluding the trade deal that has been under discussion for more than a year.

Trump said the deal "could be a much different kind of deal," hinting that the agreement between India and the US could differ from earlier trade pacts.

"They want to make a deal. We’re going to make a deal. Pretty close, yeah," Bloomberg cited Trump as he addressed journalists at the White House.

Trump's remarks come while US Secretary Marco Rubio is on a two-day visit to India. The visit is widely seen as an attempt by Washington to repair relations amid tensions between the US and India over visa restrictions and tariff threats.

Alleviating concerns, Rubio on Tuesday said the tariffs are not meant to "punish India" and the visa restrictions are "not targeted" at the country.

"I think we’re incredibly close. The way I would say it is, we are weeks, not months, away from, I think, finalising it. I think 99% of the work is done. The remaining factor, you have to have 100% done. But I feel very positive of the trajectory that it’s on," he said in an interview with Indian newspaper The Indian Express.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from DW's New Delhi Bureau bringing you all the important updates from across India.

India is hosting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on his second official visit to the country this year. Rubio, who arrived in Mumbai, met Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar on Tuesday.

During the meeting, Rubio and Jaishankar exchanged views on various topics, including trade, defense, technology and energy security. Following his meeting with Jaishankar, Rubio said that the India-US trade deal is "incredibly close."

Today, Rubio is scheduled to visit the world's largest oil refinery, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, in the western state of Gujarat.

Meanwhile, the United Nations has taken note of the crackdown on protests in the past few weeks and urged Indian authorities to cease the use of "excessive force" against unarmed protesters.

Stay tuned as we bring you more deets from India.

entries.title: Musk says SpaceX-Tesla merger 'good idea' as companies explore union
entries.summary: Musk confirmed the long standing speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX but warned that it would be premature to assume it is happening for sure.
entries.content:
October 21, 2026

Musk confirmed the long standing speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX but warned that it would be premature to assume it is happening for sure.

Tech billionaire Elon Musk on Tursday said a merger between his two companies, SpaceX and Tesla, would be a "good idea" and that they had formed special committees to discuss the matter — confirming speculation of a possibly union.

"I think it would be a good idea, but it's really up to the special committees of both companies," Musk said.

"Because ​I'm a conflicted party, I can't actually be in the discussions of the special committees," which was comprised of independent directors, he told investors on a conference call.

Shares of the space tech company rose 8% in trade over Musk's comment, while Tesla's shares rose 1.8%. The space tech company had earlier posted its first profit as a public company.

About that, Musk said he expected an annual recurring revenue between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027, as demand for its data enter space surges and the AI boom.

Merger not a given

This is not the first time Musk has publicly spoken about a merger between his auto-making and rocket-making companies.

Speculation about a possibly merger gained traction recently with Barclays suggesting that a deal could be announced before Tesla's annual meeting in December.

Musk told investors that the special committees has been formed at the request of shareholders who would ultimately need to approve a deal. At least 50% of Tesla shareholders would have to approve a deal for it to go through.

"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and ​there's a lot to be ‌gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity," he said.

He added a disclaimer that it would be premature to assume a merger would happen.

What investors are saying

"Going into this, I'd have said there's a 90% chance that something happens in the next two years. It's a 95% chance, I think, now. It might even be in the next year. But clearly there is momentum around this internally and I think that ‌ultimately it does happen," said Gene Munster, Managing Partner at Tesla Investor Deepwater Asset Management.

Justus Parmar, Chief Executive Officer at Frotuna Invesments said there was another benefit to the deal apart from having all of Musk's companies in one place for investors to back.

"Tesla runs a high-margin, cash-generative automotive business and there's more growth to come with the robotaxis on the way. That cash flow could help support SpaceX's bottom line and fund its very capital-intensive space exploration and launch goals, including orbital data centers," he said.

Edited by: Kieran Burke

entries.title: Rising emissions and temperatures: The cost of Trump's climate retreat is now clear
entries.summary: The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.
entries.content:
October 21, 2026

The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.

For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.

That goal is no longer within reach.

Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.

If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes. 

The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.

Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

The outlook has worsened in part because of US President Donald Trump's withdrawal of the United States from the historic Paris climate accord in which the world came together in 2015 to agree to halt climate change. The US is the second-largest annual emitter of climate-warping greenhouse gases.

Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.

"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.

What does overshooting mean for the planet?

Exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius even temporarily sets humanity on a dangerous course, as it increases the risk of triggering potentially irreversible or difficult-to-undo "tipping points," like the loss of coral reefs, long-term retreat of ice sheets, and the Amazon Rainforest turning into a grassland.

As ecosystems disappear and sea levels rise, these changes could trigger a deadly chain reaction, releasing more greenhouse gases and accelerating warming, dramatically increasing the likelihood of deadly extreme weather.

This summer alone, Europe recorded more than 32,000 excess deaths related to heat and nearly 1,500 people died in a flash floods in Nepal and Tibet, after climate change laid the groundwork for a glacier to collapse.

But scientists maintain 1.5 degrees Celsius is not a magic number, and that every fraction of a degree of warming brings escalating risks. To reduce the risk of future damage, countries should still focus on rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels, the largest contributor to global climate change, and toward renewable energy like solar and wind.

Now the best-case scenario is overshooting 1.5 degrees Celsius for a short time before bringing temperatures back down quickly.

"Overshoot is not surrender," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a press statement. "We can still keep it as small and as short as possible — and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees before the end of the century."

How can the world limit overshoot?

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.

It would also require removing 330 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and storing it in the ground. But recent studies have cast doubt on the feasibility and costs of the technology, as well as the nascent carbon removal industry's ability to scale as quickly as required to meet climate goals. 

The UN warns any delays will make the challenge harder, saying that every five years that emissions remain at current levels adds about 0.1 Celsius to projected peak warming.

"We must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 Celsius by the end of the century," Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP, said in a press release. "This is possible."

Climate policy works

Still, climate policies have proven effective in reducing emissions. The UNEP report draws on more than 200 studies that analyze how measures like carbon taxes, government climate targets, building codes and subsidies for low-carbon technologies are working. 

Carbon-pricing schemes have been the most widely studied so far. China's pilot schemes reduced emissions by about 11%, while the European Union's emissions trading system saw an 8% cut, compared with projected levels without these policies. 

"There are more opportunities than ever to accelerate action," according to the report, pointing to the boom in renewable energy since the adoption of the Paris Agreement a decade ago.

Global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, and solar build-out grew seven times faster. In 2024, more than 90% of renewable projects were cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

While total energy supply from coal, oil and gas has continued to rise, that's happened at a slower rate than was projected in 2015. And coal use is likely to peak and decline by the end of the decade.

"We have a wealth of success stories showing that emissions can be cut quickly," Andersen said. "It is now up to nations to urgently put in place policies that spark fast, deep and sustained emissions reductions, and put the world on track for a more stable climate and more stable economies and societies."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins
